scenes.purpose: Open on the claim in a creator's own words.

visual.description: Quote card: the definition types on as spoken; 'without pesticides' turns amber.
onScreenText: "organic mean it means without pesticides herbicides fungicides and insecticides"

scenes.direction: Cold open; hold half a second after the last word.
scenes.narration: Dr. Eric Berg puts it in one breath: "what does organic mean it means without pesticides herbicides fungicides and insecticides".

scenes.purpose: Pose the two questions the video answers.

visual.description: The first question types on, large and centred; 'spray' holds in amber.
onScreenText: What are organic farmers actually allowed to spray?

scenes.direction: Type on with the narration; beat after the question mark.
scenes.narration: So what are organic farmers actually allowed to spray? And if they do spray, does eating organic still keep pesticides out of you?

scenes.purpose: A second creator repeats the claim, then the video turns to the rulebook.

visual.description: Quote card: the words appear as spoken; 'not been sprayed' turns amber, then the card slides away on 'rulebook'.
onScreenText: "a food that has technically not been sprayed"

scenes.direction: Card exits on s05 ahead of the excerpt.
scenes.narration: Dr. Mindy Pelz describes organic produce as "a food that has technically not been sprayed". The quickest way to check is to read the rulebook itself.

scenes.purpose: Show the US rule that allows spraying once prevention fails.

visual.description: The US regulation paragraph scrolls in; the permission clause highlights as it is read.

excerpt.highlight: may be applied to prevent, suppress, or control pests, weeds, or diseases

scenes.direction: Highlight sweeps on the quoted words.
scenes.narration: The US organic regulations say that when a farm's preventive practices are not enough, a biological or botanical substance, or a synthetic one from an approved national list, "may be applied to prevent, suppress, or control pests, weeds, or diseases".

scenes.purpose: Show that the list is of allowed synthetics, and that Europe's list holds sprays too.

visual.description: The heading of the US National List section, its title highlighted; the EU list is named in the citation as the narration moves to Europe.

excerpt.highlight: Synthetic substances allowed for use in organic crop production

scenes.direction: Highlight on the heading as it is read; hold through the EU half.
scenes.narration: That list is headed "Synthetic substances allowed for use in organic crop production", so not even every synthetic pesticide is off the table. Europe's organic list is no purer: it names paraffin oils, lime sulphur and copper compounds such as Bordeaux mixture.

scenes.purpose: Land the first finding and pivot to the safety argument.

visual.description: One line, large: 'Organic farms do spray'.
onScreenText: Organic farms do spray

scenes.direction: Punch in on 'do spray'; beat after.
scenes.narration: So organic farms do spray. The sharper argument is about whether what they spray is any gentler.

scenes.purpose: Set the two creators against each other on whether organic sprays are safer.

visual.description: Two quote cards, one per sentence: Kurzgesagt's on s09, Simnett Nutrition's on s10.
onScreenText: "Organic pesticides are not necessarily safer than conventional ones."
"they're generally not as harmful and they're more closely regulated"

scenes.narration: Kurzgesagt tells its viewers, "Organic pesticides are not necessarily safer than conventional ones." Simnett Nutrition takes the other side: "they're generally not as harmful and they're more closely regulated".

scenes.purpose: Show how small the organic list is next to Europe's full pesticide list.

visual.description: Two horizontal bars as dots: 385 for all EU-approved substances, then 26 for those also approved for organic.

chart.title: Pesticide substances approved in the EU
chart.note: Active substances only; basic substances excluded. EU list, not the US one.

scenes.narration: A review of organic food and health went through Europe's approved list: of 385 substances authorised as pesticides in the EU, 26 are also approved for organic farming, "evaluated in accordance with the same legal framework".

scenes.purpose: Compare hazard classifications on the full and organic lists.

visual.description: Four tiles in two pairs: full list 340 and organic 10 with any identified toxicity (s12); full list 27 and organic 0 suspected human carcinogens (s13).

chart.title: Hazard classes, full list vs organic list
chart.note: Intrinsic hazard classifications, not exposure or risk.

scenes.direction: First pair on s12, second pair on s13.
scenes.narration: On the full list, 340 have some identified toxicity, meaning regulators set a safe intake or exposure limit for them; on the organic list, 10 do. And 27 substances on the full list are classed as "Suspected human carcinogens"; on the organic list, none are, and none is classed as a reproductive toxicant either.

scenes.purpose: Caveat what the hazard tables measure.

visual.description: Two lines build: 'Built-in hazard', then 'Europe's list, not America's'.
onScreenText: Built-in hazard, not how much reaches anyone
Europe's list, not America's

scenes.direction: Second line on 'only for Europe's list'.
scenes.narration: Keep in mind what those tables measure: a substance's built-in hazard, not how much of it reaches anyone, and only for Europe's list, not America's.

scenes.purpose: Show the review naming pyrethrins and copper as the exceptions.

visual.description: The review's paragraph on exceptions; the pyrethrins clause highlights on s15, the copper clause is read on s16.

excerpt.highlight: share the same mechanism of action as the synthetic pyrethroid insecticides

scenes.narration: The review also names the exceptions. Pyrethrins, an extract of a chrysanthemum, "share the same mechanism of action as the synthetic pyrethroid insecticides". And copper, a nutrient we all need, is "toxic at high intakes" and a concern for the creatures living in rivers and lakes.

scenes.purpose: Show the synthetic pyrethroids allowed only in insect traps.

visual.description: The table footnote; 'insect traps' highlighted as it is said.

excerpt.highlight: approved for use in certain insect traps in organic agriculture

scenes.narration: Europe's organic rules even allow a pair of synthetic pyrethroids, but only inside insect traps, where the review judges the risk of them reaching food negligible.

scenes.purpose: Answer the first question.

visual.description: One line slams in: 'Organic does not mean unsprayed'.
onScreenText: Organic does not mean unsprayed

scenes.narration: So organic does not mean unsprayed. In America the rules allow listed sprays once prevention has failed; in Europe, where the hazard tables come from, the organic list is mostly of low concern on those tables, with pyrethrins and copper as the real exceptions.

scenes.purpose: Pose the second question.

visual.description: The question types on; 'inside you' turns amber.
onScreenText: Does eating organic change what ends up inside you?

scenes.narration: Which leaves the question most shoppers really care about: if organic farms spray too, does eating organic change what ends up inside you?

scenes.purpose: The strongest version of the residue claim.

visual.description: Quote card; 'no pesticide residues' turns amber.
onScreenText: "the primary advantage of organic produce is that there are no pesticide residues"

scenes.narration: In a DW Documentary film, one interviewee goes further: "the primary advantage of organic produce is that there are no pesticide residues".

scenes.purpose: Challenge the quote before the data.

visual.description: The question types on, short and centred.
onScreenText: No residues at all?

scenes.narration: No residues at all? Food testing says otherwise.

scenes.purpose: European monitoring: organic samples carry residues less often, but often.

visual.description: Two bars: all samples 43.7%, organic samples 13.8%, each rising as its figure is said.

chart.title: Samples with residues within legal limits (EU)
chart.note: Averaged over three years of EFSA monitoring; 'all samples' includes organic ones.

citations.label: Mie et al. 2017, citing EFSA monitoring

scenes.narration: Averaged over recent years of European food monitoring, measurable residues within legal limits turned up in 43.7 percent of all samples, and in 13.8 percent of organic ones.

scenes.purpose: US monitoring agrees.

visual.description: One big tile: 23 percent of organic samples tested positive.

scenes.narration: American monitoring data tell the same story from the other side: in the federal Pesticide Data Program, 23 percent of organic samples still tested positive.

scenes.purpose: The meta-analysis puts the gap side by side.

visual.description: Two bars: conventional 46%, organic 11%; the gap between them is the beat.

scenes.narration: A meta-analysis of crop studies puts the gap at residues on 11 percent of organic samples against 46 percent of conventional ones, and an older analysis of American testing programmes found the amounts on organic samples consistently lower too.

scenes.purpose: Turn from food to body.

visual.description: The question types on; 'your body' turns amber.
onScreenText: What actually ends up in your body?

scenes.narration: Residues on food are one thing, though. What actually ends up in your body?

scenes.purpose: The light-switch claim.

visual.description: Quote card; 'like a light switch' turns amber.
onScreenText: "turn on and off urinary concentrations of pesticide metabolites like a light switch"

scenes.narration: NutritionFacts.org says you can "turn on and off urinary concentrations of pesticide metabolites like a light switch".

scenes.purpose: The trials back it: urinary pesticide metabolites fall fast.

visual.description: One tile: up to 90% reduction during the organic phase, arriving on s28.

chart.title: Whole-diet organic trials, urine tests
chart.note: Four trials; exposure, not health outcomes.

scenes.narration: That sounds like hype, but a systematic review backs it: all four trials it found that swapped people's whole diet to organic and tested their urine, two in children and two in adults, found pesticide breakdown products fell significantly. The drop was often dramatic, as much as 90 percent, and it came within a few days.

scenes.purpose: Caveat: exposure is not health.

visual.description: One line: 'Exposure, not health'.
onScreenText: Exposure, not health

scenes.narration: What these trials measure is exposure, not health, and a review of farming systems notes that lower residues may not translate into better health outcomes.

scenes.purpose: Answer the second question.

visual.description: Two lines build: lower sharply and quickly; not entirely.
onScreenText: Sharply and quickly lowers
Does not get rid of either entirely

scenes.direction: Second line on 'does not get rid of'.
scenes.narration: So yes: eating organic sharply and quickly lowers the pesticides on your food and in your body, but it does not get rid of either entirely, and whether that makes you healthier is a separate question this evidence leaves open.

scenes.purpose: Bring the two answers together.

visual.description: Split field: 'The field' on the left, 'Your body' on the right, the split closing as the slogan blurs them.
onScreenText: The field
Your body

scenes.direction: Split opens on s32's 'the field and your body'.
scenes.narration: Put both answers together and the organic label reads differently. The answers cover different ground, the field and your body, and the slogan blurs them into a promise the rulebook never makes.

scenes.purpose: Leave the viewer with the better question.

visual.description: The question types on and holds; 'which ones' turns amber.
onScreenText: Which ones, and how much of them ends up on your plate?

scenes.direction: Hold 1.5 s at the end; fade out.
scenes.narration: So the next time someone tells you organic means no pesticides, ask the better question: which ones, and how much of them ends up on your plate?
